title: Descriptive Composition (Paper 2 Section B)
description: The 0500 Paper 2 Section B descriptive composition: what the 40 writing marks reward, the establish-zoom-shift-resonate structure for 350-450 words, avoiding narrative drift, and planning under the clock.

notes.heading: The Task: One Title, 40 Marks
notes.body: Section B of Paper 2 is the composition: you choose ONE title from four — two descriptive and two narrative — and write about 350-450 words. All 40 marks are writing marks (W1-W5): there is no reading text in this section, so there is nothing to comprehend, quote or respond to except the title itself. Section A is also worth 40 marks, so the two-hour paper splits roughly in half — allow about an hour for your composition: five minutes planning, about 45 writing, five to ten checking. A descriptive title asks for a place, a moment, an atmosphere ('Describe...'), not a story. Choosing between the two descriptive options should take about a minute: pick the one where you can already see the scene.

notes.heading: What the 40 Marks Actually Reward
notes.body: Every level descriptor for composition maps to W1-W5, so translate them into behaviours. W1: a convincing, well-defined picture — ideas and images developed, not listed. W2: structure managed for deliberate effect — the mark scheme's own phrase for top-level description is 'varieties of focus': the writing moves deliberately between wide views and close detail. W3: precise vocabulary and sentence structures varied for effect, not for show. W4: language that engages the reader — one sustained atmosphere the reader can live inside. W5: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar. Marking is best-fit: the examiner finds the level your script mostly matches, then adjusts within it — so a single weakness, usually accuracy, can drag an otherwise strong piece down a level.

notes.heading: The Establish-Zoom-Shift-Resonate Structure
notes.body: Structure a descriptive piece like a camera movement, and plan it before you write. (1) ESTABLISH — the wide shot: the whole scene and one dominant mood (about 100 words). (2) ZOOM — one small detail in close-up, observed so precisely it proves you were really looking (about 100 words). (3) SHIFT — move the eye: another corner of the scene, another sense, or a change in the light (about 100 words). (4) RESONATE — a final image that echoes the opening with something changed (about 80 words). This delivers 'varieties of focus' on purpose, which is exactly what W2 rewards, and it fits the word range without padding. The sensory craft itself is taught in the KS3 Descriptive Writing topic; the exam skill is committing to this skeleton in advance, because there is no time to redraft.

illustration.alt: A four-frame storyboard of the establish, zoom, shift, resonate structure for a descriptive composition, with a word budget under each frame.
illustration.caption: Structure the piece as a camera movement: wide shot, close-up, a deliberate shift of focus, then a final image that echoes the opening.

notes.heading: Sensory Control at Speed
notes.body: Under time pressure, description fails by sprawl. Fix three things in the plan, not mid-draft: the mood word everything must serve; your lead senses — two or three, not all five, plus one unexpected detail (the smell of the rain, the taste of dust); and a bank of four to six precise images you trust yourself to write well. Then sustain: keep light and weather consistent with your mood; prefer one precise verb to two vague adjectives ('the crane pivoted' beats 'the big, tall crane moved'); and control pace with sentence length — long, layered sentences to slow the reader down, a short one to make a detail land. At this level, economy is the skill: in 400 words, every sentence must earn its place.

notes.heading: The Narrative Drift Trap
notes.body: The mark scheme names the most common failure directly: descriptive work with 'a tendency to write in a narrative style' is stuck in the middle levels for content and structure. Drift begins the moment a character DOES something consequential — a problem appears, someone acts, events queue up — and the piece becomes a story badly told rather than a place well seen. Prevention: keep the event minimal. Something may change — the light fades, a train pulls in, a crowd goes quiet — but nothing should HAPPEN in the plot sense. Paragraph self-check: did anything change, or did I simply see, hear and smell more? If a paragraph is all action verbs, you have drifted; cut the event, keep its sensory residue.

notes.heading: Planning and Checking Under the Clock
notes.body: Five minutes of planning buys the whole structure. Write down: the title, your mood word, the four beats (establish, zoom, shift, resonate), four to six concrete details, and the final image — then write straight through at roughly ten words a minute. Respect the word range: well under 350 reads as under-developed (W1); far over 450 almost always means drift or repetition, not richness. Hold back five to ten minutes for W5, the cheapest marks to protect: sentence boundaries first (comma splices are the classic leak), then apostrophes, then the spellings you know you get wrong. Check by reading slowly with your pen on each word — your eyes will skate over errors at normal reading speed.

notes.heading: Common Mistakes, and How to Practise
notes.body: The recurring failures: opening with an alarm clock, a weather report or a journey to the scene; sense-listing ('I could see... I could hear... I could smell...') instead of choosing details; adjective overload — two adjectives on every noun reads as padding, not precision; a plot breaking out halfway through; running out of time mid-zoom because there was no plan; and ignoring the word range in both directions. This quiz trains your judgement — what strong looks like and why. To train the writing itself, use this course's free-response practice sets with AI marking: write a piece in 45 minutes, study the feedback, then rewrite the SAME piece once. Rewriting against feedback is where the marks move.

flashcards.definition: Paper 2's second half: one composition from four titles — two descriptive, two narrative — about 350-450 words, 40 marks.
flashcards.example: Roughly an hour of the two-hour paper: 5 minutes planning, about 45 writing, 5-10 checking.

flashcards.definition: The mark scheme's term for moving deliberately between wide views and close detail — the signature of structured description.
flashcards.example: The whole market square, then one cracked weighing scale, then the smell of the spice stalls.

flashcards.definition: The wide opening view that fixes place, scale and one dominant mood before any detail.
flashcards.example: 'By six, the harbour had emptied of everything except light.'

flashcards.definition: The move from the wide view into one small, sharply observed detail — the close-up that proves close observation.
flashcards.example: Not 'boats in the harbour' but 'the frayed knot on the nearest mooring rope'.

flashcards.definition: A deliberate move to a new part of the scene, a new sense, or a change of light — the structure's third beat.
flashcards.example: From the stalls to the gulls; from sight to the smell of diesel and salt.

flashcards.definition: A closing picture that echoes the opening image with something changed — closure without plot.
flashcards.example: The piece opened on a lit buoy; it ends on the same light, now doubled in still water.

flashcards.definition: When a plot breaks out inside a description — events replacing observation — and pulls the piece down the levels.
flashcards.example: 'Then a fight started...' — cut the fight, keep the shout and the overturned chairs.

flashcards.definition: The small change a description may contain without becoming a story.
flashcards.example: The light fading; a train arriving; a crowd hushing — change, not plot.

flashcards.definition: The single dominant mood every detail serves; consistent light, weather and tone keep it convincing.
flashcards.example: A 'neglected' greenhouse: cracked panes, dust on the glass, one living plant.

flashcards.definition: Accuracy of spelling, punctuation and grammar — credit-bearing in every level descriptor, so the final minutes belong to it.
flashcards.example: Comma splices and apostrophes are the classic leaks; check sentence boundaries first.

flashcards.definition: The examiner matches the whole script to the closest level description, then adjusts within that level.
flashcards.example: Mostly Level 5 work with frequent accuracy errors settles in Level 4.

flashcards.definition: Title, mood word, the four structural beats, a handful of details and the final image — all decided before writing.
flashcards.example: One minute to choose the title, four to plan it; never the other way round.

questions.stem: In Paper 2 Section B, how is the composition task set?
choices: The exam board assigns one compulsory title to every candidate
You answer all four titles briefly
You choose one title from four — two descriptive and two narrative
You invent your own title on any subject
questions.explanation: Section B always offers a choice of four titles — two descriptive and two narrative — and you answer one. The other options contradict the paper's design: there is no single compulsory title, answering all four is impossible in the time, and the titles are given, not invented.

questions.stem: About how many words should a Section B composition be?
choices: About 350-450 words
About 120 words
About 550-650 words
About 800-1,000 words
questions.explanation: The composition is about 350-450 words. 120 is the word LIMIT for the Paper 1 summary task; 550-650 is the length of the Section A reading texts, not your answer; and 800+ words in the time available almost always means narrative drift or an unfinished script.

questions.stem: Which assessment objective covers accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar?
choices: W1
W5
R5
W3
questions.explanation: W5 is accuracy of spelling, punctuation and grammar. W1 is articulating experience and ideas, W3 is vocabulary and sentence variety, and R5 is a READING objective — Section B tests writing only, so no R objective is assessed here at all.

questions.stem: Section B carries 40 marks, all for writing (W1-W5). What does that imply about how you treat the title?
choices: You should analyse the wording of the title as if it were a reading text
Half the marks reward comprehension of the title
You should quote the title repeatedly to show engagement with it
There is nothing to comprehend or respond to except the title — every mark comes from the quality of your own writing
questions.explanation: Unlike Section A or Paper 1, Section B has no reading text and no reading marks — the title is a springboard, and all 40 marks judge the writing itself. Analysing the title as a text, expecting comprehension marks, or quoting it back all mistake a writing task for a reading task.

questions.stem: A student plans a descriptive piece for the title 'The bus station at dawn'. Which plan best delivers the 'varieties of focus' the top levels reward?
choices: A wide shot of the whole station, then a close-up of one cracked departure board, then a shift to the smells and sounds of the cafe grill, then a final image of the first bus's headlights
A list of everything visible, in the order the eye happens to notice it, with one sense per paragraph
The narrator arrives, misses the bus, argues with the driver and runs after it down the road
Three paragraphs of similes about the sky, each more elaborate than the last
questions.explanation: The first plan moves deliberately between wide view, close detail and a changed focus — varieties of focus by design. The list has no control of focus; the third option is a plot (narrative drift, which the mark scheme caps in the middle levels); and the fourth sustains one note with no variety at all.

questions.stem: Which paragraph signals that a descriptive piece is drifting into narrative?
choices: 'Rain glazed the pavement until the whole street shone like dark glass.'
'The fish stall smelled of salt and ice, of diesel from the idling trucks.'
'Suddenly the lights went out, the crowd screamed, and I ran for the exit, shoving past the stalls to reach my brother before the doors closed.'
'A single gull turned above the rooftops, white against the slate sky.'
questions.explanation: The third paragraph is a chain of consequential events — a problem, actions, a goal — which is plot, and plot in a descriptive piece is narrative drift. The other three are pure observation: things seen and smelled, with no event driving them.

questions.stem: Which sentence best controls atmosphere for a hushed, expectant mood?
choices: 'The hall was very quiet and everyone was waiting for the results which was tense.'
'The hall held its breath. Two hundred people, and not one cough, not one whisper — only the clock, ticking itself hoarse.'
'It was a dark and stormy night and the hall was full of people who were quiet.'
'The atmosphere in the hall was extremely atmospheric and silent.'
questions.explanation: The second sentence earns its mood: a short declarative lands, precise concrete detail replaces the abstract word 'tense', and the personification is controlled. The first is flat and vague; the third leans on a cliche and a run-on; the fourth says nothing twice ('atmospheric... atmosphere').

questions.stem: Midway through a piece describing 'A market just before closing', a student writes: 'Then a thief grabbed a purse from a stall and the trader chased him through the crowd.' What is the BEST way to rescue the piece?
choices: Keep the chase but shorten it to two sentences
Delete the whole paragraph and leave a gap
Make the thief the narrator's brother, to add emotion
Cut the chase and keep only its sensory residue — the shout, the overturned basket, oranges rolling across the stones — as observed detail
questions.explanation: Converting the event into observed residue restores description: the piece keeps the energy but drops the plot. Shortening the chase keeps the drift; deleting the paragraph leaves a structural hole; and making the thief a relative deepens the story — the exact opposite of what a descriptive task rewards.

questions.stem: A student finishes their descriptive composition at 610 words. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Narrative drift or repetitive detail — the target is about 350-450 words, and running a third over usually means the control of focus broke
Excellent development — more words always earn more W1 credit
They should add a concluding paragraph to round the piece off
Nothing — the word range is a rough guide that examiners ignore
questions.explanation: The range is 'about', but 610 words is a third over the ceiling and in timed conditions that surplus almost always comes from a plot breaking out or details repeating. Volume is not development (W1 rewards a convincing picture, not a long one), adding more would worsen it, and the range is part of the task, not decoration.

questions.stem: Paper 2 is two hours for 80 marks — Section A (40) and Section B (40). Which time budget best fits the composition?
choices: About 15 minutes — the composition is a short task
About 90 minutes — the composition should take most of the paper
About an hour: five minutes planning, about 45 writing, five to ten checking
No planning — start writing immediately to maximise the word count
questions.explanation: Equal marks means roughly equal time: about an hour for Section B, split plan-write-check. Fifteen minutes starves a 40-mark task; ninety minutes bankrupts Section A; and skipping the plan sacrifices W2 (structure) and usually W5 (accuracy), which together cost more than a few extra sentences gain.

questions.stem: A piece describing 'The beach after the storm' opens with 'a single red bucket, upright on the empty sand'. Which closing line best completes the structure?
choices: 'And then I went home and had tea.'
'The tide had turned. The red bucket lay on its side now, half-buried, already becoming part of the beach.'
'Suddenly an enormous wave came and destroyed the entire beach.'
'In conclusion, the beach after the storm is a very descriptive place.'
questions.explanation: The second line is the resonant final image: it returns to the opening image with something changed, which gives closure without plot. The first is bathos; the third invents a disaster — narrative drift in the final line; the fourth slips into essay voice, abandoning the descriptive register entirely.

questions.stem: A plan for 'The library at closing time' reads: 'Paragraph 1: the shelves. Paragraph 2: I discover a hidden door. Paragraph 3: the corridor beyond it. Paragraph 4: what I find there.' What is wrong with this plan?
choices: Libraries are an unsuitable subject for description
Four paragraphs are too many for 350-450 words
The plan has no concluding paragraph
It is a plot, not a description — discovery, exploration and revelation are events, and the focus never settles on observation
questions.explanation: The plan is structured around things HAPPENING — a hidden door, a corridor, a discovery — so the piece will be marked as narrative-style writing and capped in the middle levels. Libraries are fine subjects, four paragraphs fit the word count well, and a description needs a resonant final image rather than a formal conclusion.

questions.stem: You have six minutes left at the end of the paper. Which check is worth the most marks?
choices: Sentence boundaries and spelling — W5 accuracy is credit-bearing in every level descriptor
Adding one more simile to paragraph two
Rewriting the opening sentence in a more ambitious style
Counting the words twice to be safe
questions.explanation: W5 runs through every level descriptor, so hunting comma splices and misspellings protects marks you have already earned. A late simile adds risk rather than credit, rewriting the opening endangers the whole piece for one sentence, and recounting words changes nothing.

questions.stem: In a descriptive composition, the 'event' of the piece should be:
choices: As dramatic as possible — a chase or a disaster
Minimal — the light may change or a train may arrive, but no plot should break out
A complete story with a twist ending
Excluded entirely — nothing may change at any point
questions.explanation: A minimal event gives the piece movement without plot: change, not story. Drama and twist endings are narrative techniques — drift in a descriptive task — while forbidding any change at all overshoots; a shifting light or an arriving train is exactly the kind of small change that animates description.

questions.stem: You must choose between the two descriptive titles in about a minute. Which should a strong candidate pick?
choices: The most original-sounding title, because originality is rewarded
The shorter title, because short titles are easier to answer
The title for which they can already see the scene — a place they can picture with senses attached
A narrative title instead, because stories are easier to structure
questions.explanation: Title choice is about available material: the scene you can already picture comes with details attached, and details are what description lives on. Originality of the title earns nothing — the writing is marked, not the choice; title length is irrelevant; and abandoning description for a narrative ignores the advice to play to the material you can see.
